items.headline: Deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack', Macron says
items.blurb: One person is killed and five wounded in a series of attacks. The suspected gunman has been apprehended.
items.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack". Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this. The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested. Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition. Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root". The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise". items.headline: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
items.blurb: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth…
items.text: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda , Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added. The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history. items.headline: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
items.blurb: Thirty-four people are also injured in the attack in southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.
items.text: Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said. At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday. The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack. In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists". Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties". Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven. CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church. items.headline: WHO announces start of Ebola vaccine clinical trial in DR Congo
items.blurb: A clinical trial begins to test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
items.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced the beginning of the first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak that started in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). WHO’s director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a social media post on Friday that participants in the trial were vaccinated with the Ervebo vaccine in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak. Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial to see if it offers any cross-protection against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola that is behind the epidemic. “This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” the WHO chief said on X. “WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives,” he added. items.text: Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s . The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record. Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993. Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. items.headline: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
items.blurb: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.
items.text: Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention. Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022. "We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days." Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers. "It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read." Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner. It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.” The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week. items.headline: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead
items.blurb: The soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint outside the West Bank city on Friday morning.
items.text: The Israeli military has begun demolishing Palestinian buildings in the city of Hebron, after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would "destroy" the neighbourhood where the two attackers came from, and that Israel was ready for "extensive action" in the occupied West Bank. Three other soldiers were wounded in the attack at a checkpoint outside Hebron, before the gunmen were shot dead, officials say. It comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days' time. Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen. Other footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire. The latest extension of flight cancellations follows a series of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), including a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam that killed an Indian national and injured two others, and a separate attack on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield that injured another Indian national. #TravelAlert IndiGo flights to and from Riyadh will remain cancelled until 31 October 2026 (inclusive), while flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah will remain cancelled until 27 October 2026 (inclusive). items.blurb: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman has urged regulators to speed up refunds of unclaimed bank deposits, shares, dividends, insurance and pension funds.
items.text: Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday urged financial sector regulators to expedite refunds of unclaimed assets to their rightful owners, simplify know-your-customer (KYC) processes and strengthen cybersecurity preparedness amid rising geopolitical uncertainties. The issues were discussed at a meeting of the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC), the apex body for inter-regulatory coordination in the financial sector, chaired by Sitharaman. The Council took note of the Financial Sector Cyber Security Strategy (FSCSS), formulated by an inter-ministerial group comprising financial sector regulators and cybersecurity agencies, according to a finance ministry statement. Mandated by the Council in August last year, the strategy envisages regulatory harmonisation and unified cybersecurity standards across the financial sector. It also seeks to strengthen risk management frameworks for emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and quantum technologies, while improving the resilience of third-party service providers. “The implementation of the FSCSS is expected to strengthen the overall resilience of the Indian financial sector,” the statement said. items.blurb: Organised by the Disha Students’ Organisation and Bhagat Singh Jan Adhikar Yatra (BSJAY), the demonstration also called for the repeal of the 2023 law governing the appointment of Election Commissioners
items.text: Disha student organisation organised a protest outside the University of Mumbai, Kalina, demanding the scrapping of SIR and the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar. Students, activists and working professionals staged a protest outside Mumbai University’s Kalina campus on Friday (October 23, 2026), demanding the complete withdrawal of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the arrest of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and fresh elections based on previous voter lists. Organised by the Disha Students’ Organisation and Bhagat Singh Jan Adhikar Yatra (BSJAY), the demonstration also called for the repeal of the 2023 law governing the appointment of Election Commissioners. Protesters alleged that the electoral roll revision exercise threatened voting rights, particularly those of marginalised communities, and accused the Election Commission of India (ECI) of acting in the BJP’s interests. Addressing the gathering, Dr. Pooja, coordinator of BSJAY, alleged that the SIR could disenfranchise Muslims, Dalits, Adivasis and working-class voters. She questioned the Election Commission’s independence and accused Mr. Kumar of misusing his authority to benefit the ruling party. items.blurb: Union minister Ashwini Vaishnav said the time has come when the risks of AI have crossed a threshold when we should come up with a law.
items.text: Union minister for railways, information and broadcasting, and electronics and information technology Ashwini Vaishnaw on Friday said the government will issue a consultation paper on a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) law “in coming weeks”, saying the risks from the technology have crossed a “threshold” that now demands legislation. Speaking at the NDTV World Summit in Delhi, Vaishnaw said the proposed regulation will target the harms of AI while keeping humans in control of the technology. “Today the time has come when the risks of AI have crossed a threshold when we should come up with a law,” Vaishnaw said. “We should come up with a new regulation where the harms from the new technology can be regulated. Having said that, we are already working on it.” The remarks mark a visible shift in the government’s public stance. The IT ministry’s India AI Governance Guidelines, released on November 5, 2025, called for focused amendments to existing laws instead of a standalone AI statute. items.headline: Trinidad and Tobago in talks with ONGC Videsh, Oil India to refine Venezuelan crude
items.blurb: The Caribbean government has proposed that the two Indian oil companies process crude from neighbouring Venezuela at the Guaracara refinery in Pointe-à-Pierre, which forms part of the former Petrotrin complex and is currently under renovation.
items.text: New Delhi: Trinidad and Tobago is in talks with state-run ONGC Videsh Ltd (OVL) and Oil India Ltd on a proposal to process Venezuelan crude at its Guaracara refinery, which is being reopened after remaining shut for more than seven years, the nation’s high commissioner to India, Chandradath Singh, said in an interview. The Caribbean government has proposed that the two Indian oil companies process crude from neighbouring Venezuela at the Guaracara refinery in Pointe-à-Pierre, which forms part of the former Petrotrin complex and is currently under renovation, Singh said. Guaracara Refining Company, a subsidiary of Trinidad Petroleum Holdings, manages the refinery. “I am having discussions with them. They are very interested. They have oil wells in Venezuela, which are now opening up. We have the biggest refinery in the entire region, in Trinidad and Tobago, which was shut down for a while. But we are now reopening it,” Singh told Mint . The proposal comes as India scouts for energy supplies from across the world amid turmoil in global energy markets triggered by the war in West Asia .

items.headline: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
items.blurb: Do British pensioners have it better or worse than those in other countries?
items.text: Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic. The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011. But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade. Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people. And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while. items.headline: IRDAI to examine LIC agents’ demands as LIAFI opposes key distribution reforms ahead of October 25 deadline
items.blurb: With the feedback window closing on October 25, the coming days will show how far IRDAI is willing to adjust commission levels, disclosure rules, and clawback provisions to address LIC agents’ livelihood concerns.
items.text: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India ( IRDAI ) is set to examine seven key demands from the Life Insurance Agents’ Federation of India (LIAFI) as the agents’ body pushes back against nearly every major proposal in the regulator’s planned overhaul of insurance distribution norms. The review comes just ahead of the October 25 deadline for stakeholder feedback on the consultation paper titled “Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution.” LIAFI has opposed core elements of the proposed framework, including commission caps, public disclosure of individual agents’ payouts, and provisions that would allow recovery of commissions in cases of alleged mis-selling. The federation has instead sought higher first-year and renewal commissions, arguing that the draft changes risk further squeezing agents’ already modest earnings. Specifically, LIAFI has proposed a graded first-year commission structure linked to the premium-paying term: 27 percent for policies of five to nine years, 30 percent for 10–14 years, and 35 percent for terms of 15 years and above. items.headline: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
items.blurb: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark…
items.text: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight.

items.headline: Making the case for context-aware AI
items.blurb: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one.
items.text: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can't just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. items.headline: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
items.blurb: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.
items.text: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC . This follows a similar report by Bloomberg a month ago which said the AI lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change. CNBC reports that the UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, too. OpenAI declined comment.
